title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, why isn't the entire night sky blazing with light?
summary: A seemingly simple observation—that the night sky is dark—turns out to be one of the most revealing puzzles in cosmology, pointing toward the finite age of the universe itself.
content:
Look up on a clear night and you see mostly blackness punctuated by points of light. This seems obvious, unremarkable. But it is actually a profound clue about the structure of the cosmos, one that stumped astronomers for centuries and whose resolution reshaped how we think about the universe's history.

The Paradox, Stated Plainly

Imagine the universe is infinite, eternal, and roughly uniformly filled with stars. Pick any direction to look. Eventually, no matter which way you point your gaze, your line of sight must terminate on the surface of some star, just as a line drawn through an infinite forest must eventually hit a tree trunk. If that's true, every point in the sky should be as bright as the surface of a star. The whole sky should blaze like the sun, day and night. It plainly does not. Something in the assumptions must be wrong.

Wrong Guesses Along the Way

Early explanations proposed that dust clouds block distant starlight. This fails on physical grounds: dust absorbing energy for billions of years would heat up and re-radiate just as brightly. Others suggested light simply fades with distance—but the inverse-square law is deceptive here. Yes, a distant star looks dimmer, but there are also proportionally more stars at greater distances (since volume grows with the cube of distance), and these two effects exactly cancel in an infinite, static, uniform universe. The paradox survives naive fixes.

The Real Resolution

The universe is not infinite in the relevant sense and not eternal and static. It had a beginning roughly 13.8 billion years ago, which means light from stars farther than about 13.8 billion light-years has not yet had time to reach us, no matter how much space extends beyond that. Our sky is dark because our cosmic horizon is finite even if space itself is infinite. Additionally, the universe is expanding, redshifting the light from very distant, very old sources into wavelengths we cannot see, further dimming what does arrive. Olbers' paradox turns out to be indirect observational evidence for the Big Bang, discovered as a pure thought experiment long before the physics of cosmic expansion was understood.

Why a Simple Observation Carried So Much Weight

What makes this puzzle remarkable is how much cosmology can be extracted from something anyone can notice by stepping outside at night. No telescope, no equation—just the color of the sky—implies that the universe has a finite age and a finite reachable extent. It is a reminder that foundational truths about reality sometimes hide in observations so ordinary that no one thinks to interrogate them.

An Echo in Radio and Beyond

The same logic that explains the dark night sky in visible light also explains why the cosmic microwave background—the afterglow of the early universe—appears as a nearly uniform glow at radio wavelengths rather than something we'd see with our eyes: it is simply the most distant "surface" we can see, redshifted by cosmic expansion into microwaves. In a sense, the sky isn't truly dark at all; we are blind to the wavelength at which it blazes brightest.

perspectives.title: Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: Star density, distance, and the inverse-square law combine in a way that only makes sense once you accept a finite cosmic horizon rather than an eternal, infinite starfield.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is indirect but powerful evidence that the universe had a beginning—an argument reached from an armchair, decades before redshift surveys or the cosmic microwave background confirmed it.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The puzzle passed through Kepler, Halley, and Olbers over centuries, each adding a piece, showing how long a deceptively simple question can resist a full explanation.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: It's a textbook case of how a null observation—something NOT happening—can be as scientifically informative as a positive detection, if you take the absence seriously enough to demand an explanation.
